paragraphs: COPML addresses a collaborative learning problem: several data owners want to train one logistic regression model while keeping their individual datasets private from one another. The paper aims to make this collaboration scalable as well as private, so distributing work across additional participants can help with the computational burden.

The framework securely encodes each owner's data and distributes computation across the participating parties. Both training calculations and model updates operate on those encoded data in a fully decentralized arrangement. This makes secure encoding part of the computational organization of training, rather than merely a way to protect data during transfer.

The authors analyze privacy and prove convergence of the training procedure. Their protocol provides statistical privacy guarantees against colluding adversaries even when those adversaries have unbounded computing power. Experiments report training speedups of up to sixteen times over the benchmark protocols. These results support the possibility of combining privacy protection with substantial computational gains in the collaborative logistic regression setting studied.
neurips-2020-a-scalable-approach-for-pri.tldr: COPML distributes logistic regression training over securely encoded data, providing statistical privacy guarantees and reported speedups of up to sixteen times.

paragraphs: This paper studies repeated choices among resources that become temporarily unavailable after use. Rewards can change adversarially, without following a probability distribution. A decision therefore affects both the reward collected now and which resources will be available later, capturing allocation problems in which supplies need time to replenish.

Even when all rewards and blocking durations are known beforehand, finding the best sequence of choices is strongly NP-hard. Unless P equals NP, the problem also rules out a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme. The authors nevertheless establish an approximation guarantee for choosing the best available resource greedily, with its quality depending on blocking durations and reward variation.

For unknown rewards and durations, the paper introduces RGA when the variation budget is known and RGA-META when it is not. Their dynamic approximate regret guarantees require bounded blocking durations and bounded reward variation. If either is unbounded, the authors prove a linear lower bound on approximate regret. They also establish tightness of RGA's upper bound when blocking durations are bounded by a constant.
neurips-2020-adversarial-blocking-bandit.tldr: The paper develops algorithms and performance limits for adversarial bandits whose chosen resources become temporarily unavailable.

paragraphs: Cycle-Contrastive Learning learns video representations through self-supervision by connecting individual frames with the videos containing them. Its starting point is the relationship between a whole video and its constituent frames. The method uses that relationship to learn correspondences across both levels, extending the focus beyond matching frames or matching clips alone.

Frame and video representations come from a single network based on an R3D architecture. A shared nonlinear transformation embeds features from both levels before the cycle-contrastive loss is applied. The training design therefore connects frame-level and video-level learning while considering contrastive representations within their respective domains. This gives the model a way to use relationships between parts and wholes as a learning signal.

The authors evaluate whether the resulting representations transfer to video understanding tasks. They report better nearest-neighbor retrieval and action recognition performance than previous methods on UCF101, HMDB51, and MMAct. These findings support the usefulness of learning frame–video relationships for representations that can subsequently serve multiple downstream tasks.
neurips-2020-cycle-contrast-for-self-sup.tldr: Cycle-Contrastive Learning uses relationships between frames and whole videos to learn representations that improve reported retrieval and action recognition results.

paragraphs: Deep Statistical Solvers learn to solve optimization problems drawn from a particular distribution of instances. Their training loss is the optimization objective itself, so training does not require a collection of answers produced by an existing solver. This removes the need to generate sample solutions before learning can begin.

The paper develops this idea using graph neural networks for systems composed of interacting, interchangeable entities, including power systems and discretized physical equations. Under sufficient conditions, the authors prove that the resulting function class can approximate the actual optimization solution to arbitrary precision. This is a statement about what the function class can represent under those conditions, rather than a guarantee that every training run finds such an approximation.

Experiments cover large linear problems and AC power grid simulations. On the power grid tasks, predictions correlate above 99.99% with Newton–Raphson outputs while running two to three orders of magnitude faster. The reported correlation and speed illustrate the practical promise of learning a solver tailored to a distribution of problems.
neurips-2020-deep-statistical-solvers-72.tldr: Deep Statistical Solvers train directly on optimization objectives, avoiding example solutions while achieving substantial reported speedups on power grid simulations.

paragraphs: Images can differ in position, color, or shape while still belonging to the same meaningful group. This paper addresses those variations directly during clustering. Instead of relying on an abstract feature representation, it learns transformations and groups images in image space, keeping the connection between the clusters and the visible images explicit.

The authors introduce two frameworks based on gradient-trained K-means and Gaussian mixture models. Each jointly learns cluster prototypes and transformations, using deep learning modules to handle spatial, color, and morphological changes. The transformation learning fits into the existing training objectives without additional losses or hyperparameters. The desired invariances can also be adapted to the task.

Because cluster centers remain image-based prototypes, the approach makes both the centers and assignments easier to interpret. Experiments show competitive results on standard image clustering benchmarks. Visualizations on real photograph collections further demonstrate robustness and the interpretability advantages. The contribution is a way to incorporate chosen image variations into clustering while preserving a visually understandable account of the resulting groups.
neurips-2020-deep-transformation-invaria.tldr: The method jointly learns image prototypes and transformations to produce interpretable clusters that account for spatial, color, and morphological variation.

paragraphs: Orthogonal Monte Carlo reduces sampling variance by imposing geometric structure on samples: their directions are orthogonal. Although the method has proved useful across machine learning applications, the paper identifies a gap between its practical success and its theoretical explanation. The authors investigate how dependence among these structured samples supports reliable estimates.

Their analysis uses the theory of negatively dependent random variables to establish new concentration results. Such results describe how estimates stay close to their targets. From these, the authors derive the first uniform convergence results for Orthogonal Monte Carlo and substantially strengthen existing guarantees for its use in kernel ridge regression. The contribution therefore connects sampling geometry to downstream learning guarantees.

The paper also introduces Near-Orthogonal Monte Carlo extensions using algebraic varieties over finite fields and particle algorithms. The authors report that these extensions consistently outperform Orthogonal Monte Carlo across the applications examined, including kernel methods and distance approximation in probabilistic metric spaces. The work thus combines a stronger explanation of an established method with proposed improvements to its sampling strategy.
neurips-2020-demystifying-orthogonal-mon.tldr: The paper strengthens theoretical guarantees for Orthogonal Monte Carlo and introduces near-orthogonal extensions with better reported application performance.

paragraphs: The paper considers parameter estimation for probabilistic generative models in a natural exponential family. Ordinary maximum likelihood can overfit with limited data and can be sensitive to noise, harming later predictions. The proposed estimator addresses these issues by allowing uncertainty about the distribution used to evaluate a candidate model.

Rather than minimizing expected log-loss for just one nominal distribution, the method minimizes the worst expected log-loss within a parametric neighborhood of that distribution. Kullback–Leibler divergence defines the neighborhood. This makes the fitting objective account for a collection of nearby distributions, so a parameter choice is assessed against the least favorable distribution in that collection.

The authors exploit an analytical expression for divergence between distributions in the same natural exponential family to make this min-max problem tractable in a broad setting, including generalized linear models. They also establish statistical consistency and report promising regression and classification results. The contribution combines a structured robustness objective with computational tractability and statistical justification within the model family studied.
neurips-2020-distributionally-robust-par.tldr: A robust maximum likelihood estimator fits exponential-family models against nearby worst-case distributions while retaining tractability and statistical consistency.

paragraphs: Glow-TTS addresses a training dependency in parallel text-to-speech generation. Earlier parallel models described in the paper need an autoregressive speech model to supply alignments between text and speech. Glow-TTS learns those alignments itself, allowing a parallel speech generation model to be trained without an external aligner.

The method combines a flow-based generative model with dynamic programming to search for the most probable monotonic alignment between text and a latent speech representation. Monotonicity preserves the order of the text as it is matched to speech. The authors find that enforcing hard alignments supports robust synthesis and generalization to long utterances, while generative flows support diverse and controllable output.

In the reported comparison, Glow-TTS synthesizes speech an order of magnitude faster than Tacotron 2 with comparable speech quality. The authors also demonstrate an extension to multiple speakers. Together, these results connect internally learned alignment with the practical benefits of parallel generation: faster synthesis while retaining quality and supporting variation in the generated speech.
neurips-2020-glow-tts-a-generative-flow-.tldr: Glow-TTS learns its own text–speech alignments and generates speech in parallel, reporting an order-of-magnitude speedup over Tacotron 2 with comparable quality.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning agents can become too specialized to the environments used during training and perform poorly in unseen ones. The paper examines data augmentation as a remedy. It finds that approaches such as cutout and random convolution make local changes to observations but have limited effectiveness in increasing diversity and improving generalization.

The proposed method, mixreg, trains on mixtures of observations from different training environments. It also interpolates the associated supervision, such as rewards, and imposes linearity constraints linking the mixed observations with that mixed supervision. This couples changes in the training inputs to changes in their learning targets. The authors describe the resulting training as increasing diversity more effectively and encouraging smoother policies.

Experiments on the Procgen benchmark show large improvements over established baselines on unseen testing environments. The method applies to both policy-based and value-based reinforcement learning algorithms. Its significance is that cross-environment mixing provides a simple training intervention with demonstrated generalization benefits, rather than requiring a separate approach for each of those algorithm families.
neurips-2020-improving-generalization-in.tldr: Mixreg combines observations and supervision across training environments to improve reinforcement learning generalization on unseen Procgen environments.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning when supervision describes groups of examples, but predictions are needed for individual examples. Multiple instance learning is one familiar version of this problem. The authors broaden the setting beyond binary classification to include multiclass classification and regression, bringing several kinds of indirect supervision into one framework.

The probabilistic formulation accommodates classification information such as pairwise similarity and triplet comparisons, as well as regression information such as group means, differences, and ranks. It enables maximum likelihood learning with models including deep neural networks and gradient boosting machines. The central idea is to connect individual predictions to the aggregate observations that are actually available during training.

The authors characterize their estimator using consistency up to an equivalence relation, allowing the convergence statement to account for solutions treated as equivalent. They establish favorable convergence properties under mild assumptions. Experiments on classification from triplet comparisons and regression from means or ranks support the approach's effectiveness, showing how several forms of group-level supervision can inform individual-level prediction.
neurips-2020-learning-from-aggregate-obs.tldr: A probabilistic framework learns individual predictions from aggregate supervision such as comparisons, group means, and ranks.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether a machine can learn reusable patterns expressed through variables directly from examples. A rule about a person moving to a place can apply across many people and places if those particulars are treated as variables. The aim is to learn this abstraction without requiring humans to pre-engineer the variables.

Unification Networks implement the idea in an end-to-end differentiable neural architecture. Their central mechanism is soft unification between examples, which lets the network generalize parts of an input into variables. The resulting invariants capture shared patterns across examples, and the network uses those patterns to solve the task. Learning the abstraction and applying it are therefore parts of the same trainable approach.

The authors evaluate the method on five datasets and show that learned invariants capture patterns in the data and can improve performance over baselines. The stated finding supports learning variable-based abstractions as a useful ingredient in neural reasoning. It does not claim that such abstractions improve every task, but demonstrates their potential through the evaluated settings.
neurips-2020-learning-invariants-through.tldr: Unification Networks learn variable-based patterns from examples through soft unification and can use those patterns to improve task performance.

paragraphs: Contrastive predictive coding can estimate mutual information by asking a critic to distinguish a positive sample from negative samples. In the multiclass formulation discussed here, the resulting estimate cannot exceed log m, where the classification problem contains m candidates. This ceiling can severely underestimate mutual information unless the number of candidates is very large.

The paper changes the classification task so that the critic must identify several positive samples jointly. This multi-label formulation can exceed the log m ceiling while using the same number of negative samples. Crucially, the authors show that the estimator remains a valid lower bound on mutual information. The change expands what the estimator can express without abandoning that theoretical interpretation.

The authors demonstrate improvements in mutual information estimation and empirical gains in unsupervised representation learning. They also report outperforming the then-current state of the art in knowledge distillation on ten of thirteen tasks. These results link the altered estimation objective to practical learning improvements, while preserving the distinction between a lower bound and an exact information estimate.
neurips-2020-multi-label-contrastive-pre.tldr: Multi-label CPC identifies multiple positive samples jointly, exceeding the usual log m ceiling while remaining a valid mutual information lower bound.

paragraphs: When task rewards are sparse, an agent needs a useful way to decide what to explore before those rewards provide much guidance. This paper builds that guidance from a learned, low-dimensional representation of the environment. The representation is trained with a combination of model-based and model-free objectives.

Novelty is measured through nearest-neighbor distances in that representation space, and those distances supply intrinsic rewards for exploration. The method then uses planning routines in the same space to pursue those rewards. Information-theoretic principles shape the representation so that the novelty signal goes beyond pixel similarity. This links the meaning of novelty to the learned encoding rather than relying solely on visual differences.

The authors evaluate the approach on several maze tasks and a control problem, reporting better sample efficiency than strong baselines. The findings support the combination of representation learning, intrinsic reward, and planning for the hard exploration settings studied. A central contribution is making the space used to measure novelty also serve as the space in which exploratory behavior is planned.
neurips-2020-novelty-search-in-represent.tldr: The method measures novelty and plans exploration in a learned representation space, improving reported sample efficiency on maze and control tasks.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning policy may solve its training task well yet fail after a small change to the task or environment. Training with manually chosen variations can help, but creating useful perturbations may be impractical or may compromise performance. This paper investigates another source of robustness: learning several successful ways to accomplish the same task.

The approach discovers diverse solutions within a single training environment, without requiring explicit environmental perturbations during training. When conditions change, it can abandon solutions that have become ineffective and adopt alternatives that still work. Diversity therefore supplies a collection of possible responses to new conditions, rather than committing training to just one successful behavior.

The authors theoretically characterize a set of environments associated with the algorithm's robustness. Empirically, they find that the diversity-driven approach can extrapolate across various environmental and task changes. These results support the claim that multiple solutions learned in one environment can help with later variation, while the theoretical characterization gives a defined setting for the robustness claim.
neurips-2020-one-solution-is-not-all-you.tldr: Learning diverse successful behaviors in one environment can help an agent adapt when task or environmental changes invalidate some of its solutions.

paragraphs: The multi-shop ski rental problem asks how to make rental and purchase decisions when shops charge different prices. A decision maker must choose when and where to buy while making decisions online. This paper studies how machine-learned advice can improve those decisions without requiring advance knowledge of how reliable that advice will be.

The authors develop both deterministic and randomized online algorithms that use either one prediction or several predictions. Their guarantees improve as predictions become better, while retaining robustness when predictors perform poorly. The algorithms do not need to know the prediction quality or the type of prediction error. This addresses the practical difficulty of using advice whose reliability is uncertain.

Experiments with synthetic data and real-world traces support the theoretical observations and show improvements over algorithms relying entirely on online decision making. The contribution combines performance benefits from useful forecasts with protection against poor ones. It also extends that balance to a setting where decisions involve choosing among shops as well as deciding when to purchase.
neurips-2020-online-algorithms-for-multi.tldr: Prediction-assisted algorithms improve multi-shop rental and purchase decisions while remaining robust to poor advice of unknown quality.

paragraphs: Online algorithms must make decisions as information arrives, and machine-learned predictions can help them anticipate what comes next. Two goals arise: consistency, meaning strong performance when predictions are accurate, and robustness, meaning a worst-case guarantee even when advice is poor. Earlier work established algorithms that trade between these goals.

This paper asks whether those trade-offs are unavoidable or merely consequences of particular algorithm designs. The authors provide the first nontrivial lower bounds for competitive analysis with machine-learned predictions. A lower bound limits what algorithms can achieve, so it can establish that a desired combination of consistency and robustness is impossible within a given setting.

The analysis focuses on ski rental and non-clairvoyant scheduling, establishing optimal trade-offs in various settings. Optimality here concerns the balance between benefiting from accurate predictions and retaining worst-case protection. The contribution therefore clarifies the limits of prediction-assisted online decision making: for the settings covered, improving one guarantee has a provably necessary cost in the other.
neurips-2020-optimal-robustness-consiste.tldr: The paper proves lower bounds and optimal trade-offs between accurate-prediction performance and worst-case protection for online rental and scheduling problems.

paragraphs: This paper examines why fitting training data exactly need not lead to poor prediction in an overparameterized linear model. It studies Basis Pursuit, which selects an exact-fitting solution with minimum L1 norm. That choice differs from the minimum L2 norm solutions emphasized in much of the earlier double-descent analysis.

The theoretical setting assumes a sparse true linear regression model and independent, identically distributed Gaussian features. Over a large range of feature counts, extending to a limit that grows exponentially with the sample count, the authors prove a high-probability upper bound on model error that decreases as features are added. The decreasing quantity is the bound; the result does not assert that every realized error decreases at every step.

The authors describe this as the first finite-sample, finite-feature analytical double-descent result for overfitting Basis Pursuit. Its bound is independent of signal strength. For sparse models with high signal-to-noise ratio, its descent floor can also be substantially lower and wider than that of minimum L2 norm solutions, revealing a meaningful difference between the two fitting rules.
neurips-2020-overfitting-can-be-harmless.tldr: Under sparse Gaussian regression assumptions, Basis Pursuit has a decreasing error upper bound across a broad but bounded overparameterized regime.

paragraphs: Pontryagin Differentiable Programming connects learning with optimal control by calculating how a system's trajectory changes when tunable parameters change. Those parameters can belong to the system dynamics, its policy, or its control objective. This provides a common route to end-to-end learning across several kinds of control problems.

The framework differentiates through Pontryagin's Maximum Principle to obtain analytical trajectory derivatives. It also constructs an auxiliary control system for the backward pass. The output of that auxiliary system is the derivative of the original trajectory with respect to the parameters, and standard control tools can solve it iteratively. This turns the derivative calculation itself into a control problem that existing methods can address.

The authors investigate inverse reinforcement learning, system identification, and control or planning within this framework. Demonstrations include a multi-link robot arm, a six-degree-of-freedom quadrotor, and a six-degree-of-freedom rocket landing system. These examples demonstrate the framework's capabilities across different learning modes and high-dimensional systems, supporting its role as a shared methodology for learning and control.
neurips-2020-pontryagin-differentiable-p.tldr: Pontryagin Differentiable Programming computes trajectory derivatives through optimal control conditions to support end-to-end learning of dynamics, policies, and objectives.

paragraphs: Neural classifiers can struggle when some labels dominate the training data or when the testing distribution differs from training. This paper approaches label imbalance and shifts in label frequency through the perspective of an optimal Bayes classifier. It derives a prior rebalancing method formulated as a Kullback–Leibler divergence optimization problem.

The method includes a flexible hyperparameter that can be tuned efficiently on validation data after training. Adjusting it changes the classifier margin to address imbalance. The authors also combine prior rebalancing with existing methods for likelihood shift, interpreting both through the same Bayesian framework. This produces a unified approach to the two problems that can be used with probabilistic classifiers across different architectures.

Evaluations span six datasets and five architectures, with reported state-of-the-art accuracy. They include large-scale imbalanced classification on iNaturalist and semantic segmentation on Synthia. These findings support the practical usefulness of post-training recalibration and its combination with likelihood-shift methods, while showing applicability across both image-level classification and pixel-level prediction.
neurips-2020-posterior-re-calibration-fo.tldr: A Bayesian post-training recalibration method rebalances class priors and combines with likelihood-shift methods to improve predictions on imbalanced datasets.

paragraphs: This paper investigates robust reinforcement learning through a sampling perspective. The objective is to train agents that generalize across differences between training and testing conditions. Its proposed approach uses Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics within a two-player reinforcement learning algorithm, bringing sampling into the adversarial training process.

The algorithm is a scalable sampling variant of two-player policy gradient. The central methodological change is therefore in how the learning procedure operates: it uses Langevin-based sampling within the two-player framework. This offers a route to robustness through the training procedure, with the paper examining whether the resulting agents handle changed conditions more successfully.

Experiments on several MuJoCo environments show consistently better generalization than the existing baselines considered. The authors also report substantial robustness relative to standard reinforcement learning algorithms even when the objective functions entirely ignore possible environmental shifts. That finding is particularly relevant to the method's motivation: in the evaluated settings, the sampling approach provides robustness benefits even without explicitly representing those shifts in the objective.
neurips-2020-robust-reinforcement-learni.tldr: A Langevin-sampling variant of two-player policy gradient improves reported robustness and generalization across several MuJoCo environments.

paragraphs: This paper develops a way to learn shape representations from 3D point clouds while handling geometric transformations, especially rotation. Its aim is to capture useful information about an object without requiring explicit data augmentation for those transformations. This matters because a change in an object's orientation changes its point coordinates while preserving its shape.

The approach builds its representation from local information toward a description of the whole object. Graph convolutional neural networks produce a hierarchy of descriptors: learned summaries that encode rotation-invariant shape information at multiple levels of abstraction. This bottom-up structure connects information at different scales, giving the model a way to represent shape beyond a single level of detail.

At each level, the method uses stochastic sampling of 3D points to obtain graph-based descriptors. The authors report that this helps make the learned representations robust to input variations. They also report state-of-the-art performance on rotation-augmented benchmarks for object recognition and segmentation, supporting the approach's usefulness for both identifying objects and separating their constituent regions. Ablation experiments further examine the algorithm's characteristics.
neurips-2020-rotation-invariant-local-to.tldr: A hierarchy of graph-based shape descriptors learns rotation-invariant point-cloud representations without explicit transformation augmentation, achieving reported state-of-the-art recognition and segmentation results.

paragraphs: Worst-case analysis can make online decision problems look pessimistic when actual inputs contain useful patterns. Predictions learned from past inputs may exploit those patterns, but they can also be arbitrarily poor. This paper develops algorithms that use predictions about the future while preserving a performance guarantee when that advice is unreliable.

The authors address three settings: the classical secretary problem, online bipartite matching, and the graphic matroid secretary problem. For each, they incorporate machine-learned predictions into the online selection process. Their guarantees distinguish between the case of sufficiently accurate predictions and the case of subpar predictions, making the role of advice explicit in the analysis.

With sufficiently accurate predictions, the algorithms improve the competitive ratio over the best-known classical online algorithm for each problem. They still retain a worst-case guarantee when predictions are poor. The paper establishes a trade-off between these two competitive ratios for each algorithm. Its contribution is a quantified way to balance the benefits of accurate forecasts against protection from unreliable ones across several selection problems.
neurips-2020-secretary-and-online-matchi.tldr: Prediction-assisted secretary and matching algorithms improve guarantees with sufficiently accurate advice while retaining worst-case protection when advice is poor.

paragraphs: Predicting properties of a subgraph requires more than representing individual nodes or an entire graph. A subgraph has internal structure, a position within a larger graph, and connections to its surroundings. It may also contain disconnected components. SUBGNN is designed to learn representations that account for these features of subgraphs.

The model routes neural messages between a subgraph's components and randomly sampled anchor patches from the underlying graph. It uses three channels intended to capture distinct aspects of subgraph topology, producing representations that separate those aspects. The authors provide empirical evidence that the channels encode the properties they were designed to capture.

The evaluation introduces synthetic and real-world datasets and tests subgraph classification on eight datasets. The authors report considerable gains over strong alternatives, including node-level and graph-level methods, with a stated 19.8% improvement over the strongest baseline. SUBGNN performs particularly well on challenging biomedical datasets with complex or disconnected subgraphs, supporting the value of treating subgraphs as prediction objects in their own right.
neurips-2020-subgraph-neural-networks-9f.tldr: SUBGNN learns subgraph representations through topology-specific channels and anchor-patch messaging, improving reported subgraph classification performance.

paragraphs: Many prediction targets summarize smaller-scale events, such as national infection statistics assembled from city-level data. Models trained only on the aggregate can leave useful fine-grained information unused. This paper asks how to use both levels of information when the ultimate goal is to predict the larger-scale quantity.

The authors propose an optimization framework that fits microscopic models for macroscopic prediction using conditional stochastic optimization. It incorporates information at both scales and adapts to the individual microscopic models participating in the aggregation. This ties the fitting of the smaller-scale models to the aggregate prediction objective. The paper also develops efficient learning algorithms with convergence guarantees.

Experiments apply the framework to daily COVID-19 infection prediction and Medicare claims prediction. The authors report clear improvements over other plug-in supervised learning approaches in these real-world applications. The findings support using the relationship between detailed events and their aggregate during model fitting, showing that fine-grained modeling can improve predictions even when the quantity of interest is macroscopic.
neurips-2020-the-devil-is-in-the-detail-.tldr: The framework fits microscopic models using information at both scales to improve aggregate predictions, with convergence guarantees and positive real-world results.

paragraphs: Convolution is usually supplied as a predefined building block in vision architectures, including those found through architecture search. This paper asks whether convolution-like structure can instead emerge from learning. Its focus is the inductive bias that could encourage a fully connected image classifier to develop useful connection patterns.

The authors investigate minimum description length as a guiding principle and show that, in some settings, it can indicate architecture performance. To seek architectures with short descriptions, they introduce beta-LASSO, a simple variation of LASSO. Applied to fully connected networks, the method learns architectures with local connections, recovering an important structural feature associated with convolutional networks.

The paper reports state-of-the-art accuracies for training fully connected networks on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and SVHN: 84.50%, 57.76%, and 93.84%, respectively. These findings narrow the performance gap between fully connected and convolutional networks. The stated achievement is learning useful locality and improving fully connected classifiers; the description-length evidence is explicitly limited to some settings.
neurips-2020-towards-learning-convolutio.tldr: Beta-LASSO encourages short-description architectures that learn local connections and improve fully connected image classifiers.
